extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science/public opinion; general educated readers interested in American political culture
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive analytical criteria for identifying characteristics of American public opinion and how different social classes influence political attitudes and behaviour. Focuses on national psychological traits (e.g., commercialism, impressionability, changefulness) and class-based dispositions (farmers, shopkeepers, workers, immigrants, capitalists, professions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of serious and sustained thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of serious and sustained thinking is not confined to politics; Americans often lack minute investigation and patient reflection on underlying principles of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: vitality of certain prejudices and fallacies which continuous application of vigorous minds might dispel; Americans tend to ignore difficulties or evade them rather than 'lay siege to them according to the rules of art.' The 'sense that there is no time to spare' haunts Americans even when they might find time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/practical point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: They are a commercial people, whose point of view is primarily that of persons accustomed to reckon profit and loss, applying a direct practical test to men and measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They distrust abstract or subtle reasoning, accept only what is plain and apprehensible by ordinary understanding, assume successful men are the 'smartest,' and favor schemes which 'seem to pay well.' This practical shrewdness affects political judgement and institutional conservatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressionability of imagination and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans are impressionable not in intellect but in imagination and emotions, responding unexpectedly to appeals that seem noble or pathetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though hard to convince intellectually, Americans can display 'an ideality surpassing that of Englishmen or Frenchmen' when moved emotionally; emotional appeals can produce rapid mass adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsettled/nomadic population inhibiting durable local opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: An unsettled (often nomadic) population prevents formation of long-term habits of trustful dependence on neighbours and hinders growth of schools or types of local opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High mobility means congenial spirits seldom live together long enough to form sustained opinion or proselytizing forces; this limits the growth of variety and independent schools of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative and organizational aptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite being unsettled, Americans are strongly associative and quickly propagate sentiments; they have an aptitude for organization which produces powerful party strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each man catches his neighbour's sentiment quickly; equality of conditions and adaptability lead to rapid propagation of ideas and strong party organisation—'the immense strength of party' rests on both interest and the instinct of combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changefulness / low specific heat (sudden mass movements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans have low 'specific heat': they grow warm suddenly and cool as suddenly, liable to swift and vehement outbursts of feeling which sweep the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenomena: rapid rise and fall of movements (e.g., the Know-nothing party's quick rise and collapse) and 'Tidal Wave' elections (examples 1874-75 and 1890). Similar ideas spread rapidly because of similarity of conditions and lack of obstructing barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying conservatism despite volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans, though changeful in feeling, are fundamentally a conservative people with strong habits and tenacity toward institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roots: prosperity, pride in history and Constitution, practical recognition of value in permanence and solidity; they are ready to listen to suggestions but do not seek change for change's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmers' class characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Farmers are usually small owners, enterprising, commercially minded, not strongly rooted to a particular spot, obstinate, tenacious of habits, proud of simplicity, and suspicious of city-folk and lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political effects: primary interest in agricultural questions; susceptibility to promises of 'cheap money' or railroad regulation; tendency to support 'People's' or 'Farmer's' parties; their local agricultural press reinforces prejudices and sense of being cheated by speculators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shopkeepers and small manufacturers' traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Shopkeepers/small manufacturers form a distinct class in towns: sharper and more alive to current affairs, better educated, read more newspapers, and are more involved in local politics than farmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are less certain to be party-solid, less apt for state legislatures due to business constraints, and more likely to be interested in tariff/protection issues (Protectionists) if connected to manufacturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working men (manual wage-earners) profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Working men who toil for wages form a less well-marked class than in Europe, with distinctions between skilled and unskilled labour and many recent immigrants among unskilled workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are fairly educated, read daily newspapers, often total abstainers, move between classes frequently (easier social mobility), show less collective class feeling than in Europe, and can be more excitable and receptive to vigorous demagogues; labour agitation has roots in disparities of fortune and political influence of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorant masses / urban 'residuum' dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest urban section ('residuum')—recent immigrants, marginalized natives, Negroes—lack settled political opinions and are often massed in cities where leaders can direct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political effects: this mass can 'go solid' under leaders' direction, granting such leaders exceptional weight; they are less amenable to ordinary intellectual/moral influences and have been a decisive factor when parties are nearly balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigrant-influenced political sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain immigrant groups are influenced by religious sympathy, protection of the liquor trade, and (historically) anti-English sentiment, affecting their party alignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roman Catholic immigrants often stand by parties favourable to the Church; Germans oppose prohibition due to beer culture; Irish were swayed by dislike of England (declined after 1886). Parties have used immigrant blocs for political ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalist class levers of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalists (large merchants, manufacturers, bankers, railroad men) possess executive ability, wealth, and influence and use politics largely to protect their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means of influence: ownership/influence of newspapers, patronage of universities, control of finance and joint-stock enterprises, and informal influence over officials; they tend to be a steadying/peace party, resist sudden change that would affect markets, and split over issues like railroad control vs transport cost and tariff protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of professional men, clergy, journalists, physicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional groups have varied influence: journalists are organs of opinion, clergy engage chiefly on moral issues, and physicians typically take little active political interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy will be prominent on distinct moral questions (e.g., temperance), but in ordinary times they often avoid direct political strife; university teachers may be discouraged by wealthy patrons from promulgating disliked opinions; journalists' influence treated elsewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and class-reinforcing publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Class-specific newspapers (e.g., agricultural newspapers) write up to the prejudices of their audiences and confirm class beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the agricultural newspaper's adulation of the farming class strengthens farmers' belief that they are cheated of their fair share of prosperity and predisposes them to support legislative redress.
